text:
jordan: quick update — ran a couple of CPU-side profiles on the batching + kvcache hot path for small request workloads. trying to make sense of a perf/flamegraph run that shows surprising Python-side cost when batch sizes exceed ~64. attached artifact: /mnt/artifacts/1769001234/perf.svg

jordan: perf command used:
```
sudo perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 15
perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded
./flamegraph.pl out.folded > perf.svg
```

jordan: high level findings: 1) ~28-35% CPU attributed to Python frames (PyEval, tokenize) across workers, 2) batching scheduler functions (process_batch, schedule_worker) show up in the flame as Python frames, 3) kvcache lookup shows up but mostly in C++ (kv::lookup) and is not the dominant CPU consumer for this workload.

maya: which workload/config? prefix/kvcache enabled or disabled?

jordan: ran with prefix cache OFF for this run to isolate scheduler/tokenization overhead. I also ran a follow-up with prefix cache ON and saw similar Python overhead (slightly lower latencies but not enough to explain the delta).

sam: are you seeing GIL contention? heavy PyEval frames + futex_wait would point to threads blocked on the GIL. did perf show a lot of `futex`/`sched_yield`?

jordan: yes — perf samples include many `__lll_lock_wait`/`futex_wait` and `PyEval_EvalFrameDefault` stacks. Flame shows thick Python stacks for `process_request -> tokenize_request -> prepare_inputs` pattern. kvcache C++ code is fast but callbacks into Python for metrics/validation are non-trivial.

tina: two quick suggestions: 1) run py-spy dump to get unbiased Python stacks without nuking perf setup (no root needed), 2) micro-benchmark the tokenizer loop in isolation (move it to a tiny C++/Rust harness to compare). py-spy command:
```
py-spy top --pid <worker-pid> --native
py-spy dump --pid <worker-pid> -o pyspy.out
```

jordan: good call. py-spy showed the same stack shapes and confirms Python-level hotspots around our `batch_scheduler.py` and `tokenizer.py`. moving tokenization earlier (into C++ loader) reduced Python flame width in a quick experiment.

sam: also try sampling only user cycles to avoid kernel noise: `perf record -e cycles:u -p <pid> -g -- sleep 10`. might make symbol attribution cleaner. also consider sampling per-worker pid rather than system-wide.

jordan: noted. next steps I proposed:
- run per-worker perf cycles:u + py-spy (to correlate native vs Python)
- add a tiny microbench breaking out `tokenize_request` and `batch_scheduler` (isolated harness)
- experiment with moving tokenizer into C++ worker (pooled) or using an LRU on tokenized prefixes
- measure tail latency impact and CPU cost across batch sizes {8,32,64,128}

jordan: I've opened ENGRT-1234 and assigned to @sam to own the microbench + follow-up runs. leaving the perf.svg artifact here: `/mnt/artifacts/1769001234/perf.svg` (perf-bot uploaded it). :white_check_mark:

perf-bot: perf job finished and artifact uploaded: /mnt/artifacts/1769001234/perf.svg :robot_face:

maya: thanks — can you add the exact commit and docker image used to the issue? makes reproducing easier.

jordan: will do, adding commit sha and docker tag to ENGRT-1234. also attaching the folded stacks and raw perf script output in the issue.

tina: if we confirm GIL is the main limiter, we should prototype a non-blocking scheduler that batches work in C++ and only calls Python for final orchestration. low-effort experiment could be spawning native worker threads that run tokenization in C layer.

jordan: agreed. for now I'll run the per-worker cycles and py-spy today and post results here. thanks for the quick feedback. :thumbsup:
